title: Kulasekhara Āzhwār
body:
Chēra Nāḍu, also called Malai Nāḍu, is a land rich in wealth, encircled by great and beautiful mountains and rivers. Elephants are as plentiful there as cattle are in Tondai Nāḍu. Its people were renowned as great warriors, and not in war alone, but also in learning, in governance and in the conduct of their lives. Chēra Nāḍu was ruled for many generations by the Chēra kings, who kept it at peace and their people content.

In that line there was a king named Dṛḍhavratan, who was deeply devoted to Sriman Nārāyaṇa and who honoured the Lord's devotees with generous gifts. In reward for the king's devotion, in the year Prabhava, in the month of Māsi, on Śukla Dvādaśi, a Friday, under the Punarpūsam nakshatram, a son was born to him as an amśam of the Kaustubham, the jewel that adorns the chest of Sriman Nārāyaṇa. Born of the king's devotion to the Lord, the child shone with brightness and beauty.

The whole kingdom celebrated his birth, and on the tenth day the child was named Kulasekharan. He was as mischievous as any child, and at the same time learned all that a prince should, including Sanskrit, the language of the Vedas. Alongside his studies he was trained in the arts of war: riding horses and elephants, swordsmanship, the mace, and the chariot.

When he came of age, he ascended the throne and ruled Chēra Nāḍu even better than his father had. He honoured the devotees of Sriman Nārāyaṇa and kept his people happy. In war he was swift and fierce, and he defeated every king who opposed him. The Chōḻa and Pāṇḍya kings, jealous of his success, sought to defeat him, but Kulasekharan and his mighty army overcame them, and he extended his kingdom into the Chōḻa land.

Seeing his valour and noble bearing, the Pāṇḍya king gave him his daughter in marriage. After his marriage he continued to rule, to wage war and to conquer. But Emperumān, who reclines upon the serpent bed, wished to draw Kulasekharan out of māyā and lead him to a spiritual life.

The Turning

Kulasekharan's life went on in this way, until one day he grew weary of it and was filled with remorse for the lives he had taken in battle. This turned his thoughts to Sriman Nārāyaṇa, and he resolved to live a life of use to others and to spread devotion to the Lord among the people.

He even wished that he had not been born into wealth but into poverty, so that he might not live in luxury. He wished that he had been born a fish in one of the sacred tīrthams, so that he might live close to Perumāl.

His longing did not stop there. He imagined himself as Dēvaki, the mother of Kaṇṇan, and sang of the childhood līlās of Sri Kṛshṇa that she had never been able to enjoy:

"Thaṇ am thāmaraik kaṇṇanē! kaṇṇā!
thavazhndhezhundhu thaḷarndhōr naḍaiyāl
maṇṇil sembōḍi āḍi vandhu endhan
mārvil mannida peṭrilēn! andhō!
vaṇṇach chensiru kaiviral anaiththum
vāri vāik koṇḍa aḍisilin michchil
uṇṇap peṭrilēn, ō! keḍuvinaiyēn!
ennai en seyap peṭradhu em mōyē!"

"O Kaṇṇā, with eyes like cool, lovely lotuses! I never knew the joy of seeing You crawl, rise and toddle unsteadily, covered in the red dust of the earth, and come to rest upon my chest. Alas! I never ate the rice You scooped into Your mouth with all Your lovely little red fingers. Unfortunate that I am, why did my mother ever bear me?"

In this verse, Kulasekhara longs for Kaṇṇan as his own child and dwells on His childhood līlās, and his love for the Lord grew deeper still.

Out of his great devotion, he gave generously to the devotees of Sriman Nārāyaṇa, and he praised Perumāl by honouring and serving His devotees.

The King Who Went to War for Rāma

Kulasekharan loved to hear the stories of the Purāṇas. He invited elders to recite them and explain the truths they contained, and rewarded them generously. One day an aged yōgi was invited to narrate a story from the Purāṇas.

The yōgi told the story of the Rāmāyaṇa and of the life of Sri Rāma. As he listened, Kulasekharan was so deeply drawn to Sri Rāma that tears streamed from his eyes, and he was wholly absorbed in the Lord.

The next day the yōgi described a battle from the Rāmāyaṇa. Lakshmaṇa asked for permission to fight the rākshasas who had come against them, but Sri Rāma stopped him, asking him to stay and protect Sītā, and stepped out of the hut alone. Seeing Sri Rāma, Śūrpaṇakhā roared to the rākshasas that Rāma had come out, and urged them to surround Him. They closed in on Him on every side, sharp weapons in their hands.

So deeply was Kulasekharan absorbed in the scene that he felt some harm was about to befall Sri Rāma. He rose at once and ordered his army to prepare for war.

The army was bewildered. Whom were they to fight, when the Chōḻa and Pāṇḍya kings, their usual enemies, were quiet? But they had to obey their king, and they readied the horses and elephants for battle.

The ministers, however, understood what had happened. They realised that the king had been overcome with emotion, and they asked the yōgi to continue the story, so that Kulasekharan would learn that Rāma's battle was already won.

The yōgi finished the story: Sri Rāma, single-handed, had defeated all the rākshasas. Hearing this, and hearing of Sri Rāma's greatness, Kulasekharan was overjoyed and ordered his army back to their barracks. Such was the depth of Kulasekhara's devotion to Emperumān.

The Pot of Snakes

Days passed, and Kulasekharan became more absorbed in devotion than in ruling his kingdom.

One day he found that some of the jewels that adorned his Lord were missing, and he was angered that the ornaments had been stolen. He was determined to find the culprit. The ministers, who wished to turn the king's attention away from the Lord and His devotees, told him that the devotees of Sriman Nārāyaṇa had stolen the jewels. But Kulasekharan refused to believe it, for he had complete faith in them, and he ordered a pot filled with snakes to be brought.

He told his ministers that he would put his own hand into the pot. If the devotees of the Lord had stolen the jewels, as the ministers claimed, let the snakes bite him; if they had not, the snakes would leave him unharmed.

The Lord willed that the truth should come out. When Kulasekharan put his hand into the pot, the snakes did him no harm. The ministers then confessed the truth, and Kulasekharan required them to ask forgiveness of the devotees they had slandered. This shows how wholly Kulasekhara was devoted to Sri Vaishṇavam and to the devotees of Sriman Nārāyaṇa.
